name: Amalek
charge: Attacking Israel's stragglers on the way out of Egypt
summary: Amalek came out against Israel at Rephidim and, as Deuteronomy records, smote the hindmost, the feeble and faint and weary, and feared not God. Israel prevailed while Moses' hands were held up.
offense: This was not a stranger's war. Amalek was of Esau: Timna was concubine to Eliphaz Esau's son, and she bare to Eliphaz Amalek (Genesis 36:12), and his house were dukes in the land of Edom. So the first nation to come against Israel after the sea was a nation of their own brother's seed, which is the standing on which Edom is judged elsewhere in this volume. The manner of the attack is the charge, and Moses set it down forty years later so that it could not be forgotten: remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt, how he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God (Deuteronomy 25:17-18). He did not meet the mighty men at the front. He went to the back, where the women, the children and the old were, and took the ones who could not answer him.
judgment: The Lord swore a war without end: the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation (Exodus 17:16), and the sentence was written for a memorial in a book and rehearsed in the ears of Joshua, for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven (Exodus 17:14). Balaam pronounced the same, that Amalek was the first of the nations, but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever (Numbers 24:20). Centuries later Saul was sent by Samuel to execute it and spared Agag, and the failure is entered separately in this volume. The war then ran on exactly as sworn: David smote them and recovered all (1 Samuel 30:17-18), the sons of Simeon smote the rest that were escaped in the days of Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:42-43), and in Persia Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite (Esther 3:1), of the seed Saul had let live, rose to destroy the whole nation and was hanged on his own gallows. Generation to generation is what was sworn and what the record shows.

verses.text: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
And Moses said unto Joshua, Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek: to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand.
So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek: and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
And Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it JEHOVAH–nissi:
For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.

Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
And David smote them from the twilight even unto the evening of the next day: and there escaped not a man of them, save four hundred young men, which rode upon camels, and fled.
And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives.
And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day.
And when he looked on Amalek, he took up his parable, and said, Amalek was the first of the nations; but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever.

entries.commentary: At Rephidim there was no water, and the people did chide with Moses: wherefore is this that thou hast brought us up out of Egypt, to kill us and our children and our cattle with thirst? At the first sign of trial the people jumped off the Lord's bandwagon again, the same as we do today when tribulation comes. Moses cried unto the Lord, What shall I do unto this people? they be almost ready to stone me. They were ready to kill the prophet over water, blaming the brother for what only the Most High controls; we have to build our faith up like Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, who trusted the Lord even when trials came.

The Lord stood before Moses upon the rock in Horeb; Moses smote the rock, and water came out of it in the sight of the elders of Israel. He called the place Massah and Meribah, temptation and chiding, because they tempted the Lord, saying, Is the Lord among us, or not? That is wickedness: He had just made Egypt dark, slain their firstborn, and sent His angel in the chariot to guide us, and the people still asked whether He was with them. The mercy of the Most High in bearing that is beyond us.

Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim. Amalek was the first nation to come against Israel after Egypt; Amalek was Esau's grandson, born to Eliphaz of Timna the concubine, a duke in the land of Edom. When Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed; when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands until the going down of the sun. Moses was about eighty years old holding a rod above his head all day; the fathers were mighty men, stronger than we are today. The sign shewed the people whose hand their life was in: Moses is the man to hearken to, so do not speak against him. And Joshua discomfited Amalek with the edge of the sword; Joshua was a mighty warrior even then.

Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven. Moses wrote it, and [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25) is that rehearsal: remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way. Amalek smote the hindmost, all that were feeble, when Israel was faint and weary, and he feared not God. He did not meet the mighty men in the front; he went to the back to slay the women, the children, and the old ones. That same spirit works against the nation's young and old today. The Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation. By the time Moses rehearsed it in Deuteronomy, forty years had passed and the children of Amalek had done nothing themselves; hundreds of years after that the Lord sent Saul by Samuel to smite Amalek for what was done coming out of Egypt. God be true and every man a liar: the nations do not get away with what they did to His people, and the judgment carries to the seed. Saul did not finish Agag's line, and in Esther's day Haman the Agagite of that same seed rose against Israel; the war truly runs from generation to generation. Today that seed says they are Jews and are not, but are the synagogue of Satan, robbing Israel of identity and prospering off the oppression. The Lord says He will make them come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee. The whole world is set up between Jacob and Esau, and Esau is the end of this world, the so-called white man, with Amalek leading; it is not speaking of the Arab man, for if Ishmael had a rulership still to come, Israel would have another captivity to enter, and Christ has already redeemed us from the curse of the law. The enmity was set from the garden between the serpent's seed and the woman's seed. They bruised Christ's heel, but at the end of the world Jacob bruises the head: the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly.

If there be a controversy between men, the judges justify the righteous and condemn the wicked; the wicked man worthy to be beaten was made to lie down and be beaten before the judge's face, according to his fault, by a certain number. Forty stripes may he give him, and not exceed, lest thy brother should seem vile unto thee. Paul recounted receiving that beating under this law.

Thou shalt not muzzle the ox when he treadeth out the corn: the corn is the reward for the ox. Paul applies this verse to how the elders are treated: let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine, for the labourer is worthy of his reward. Giving double honour is not just saying the words to the leadership; it is true respect and reverence toward the leadership that labours in this word and doctrine.

If brethren dwell together and one of them die and have no child, the wife of the dead was not to marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother took her to wife, and the firstborn she bare succeeded in the name of the dead brother, that his name be not put out of Israel. Check this out: this is no longer the law, so do not try to use it as an excuse toward your brother's wife. It stood for the name not being put out because of the land inheritance in Israel. The man who refused was called before the elders; his brother's wife loosed his shoe from off his foot, spat in his face, and answered, So shall it be done unto that man that will not build up his brother's house; and his name was called in Israel, The house of him that hath his shoe loosed.

Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt: he met thee by the way and smote the hindmost of thee, all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary, and he feared not God. Israel was later commanded through Samuel to repay it: I remember that which Amalek did to Israel; now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not. At Rephidim, where Amalek first came and fought with Israel, the Lord told Moses to write this for a memorial in a book and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, for the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation; and that war is still going on even to this day.

Samuel said unto Saul, The Lord sent me to anoint thee to be king over his people; now therefore hearken thou unto the voice of the words of the Lord. Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way when he came up from Egypt. Generations after the wilderness, the Most High still remembers; the generation of Amalekites had returned, and it was time to fulfil what was written. Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass. This is a specific instruction: kill all of them, spare none. Note that the Most High commanded this against a generation that had not personally done the deed in the wilderness; that answers the argument, I never did anything to you, so why hold it against me? The Most High himself commanded recompense for what was done to the forefathers. Christianity says forgive and forget, but the Most High God said remember; this is a righteous grudge, and it shows [Leviticus 19:18](/bible/leviticus/19#v18) applies to the children of thy people.

Saul gathered the people and numbered them in Telaim, two hundred thousand footmen and ten thousand men of Judah, and laid wait in the valley. Saul said unto the Kenites, Go, depart, get you down from among the Amalekites, lest I destroy you with them: for ye shewed kindness to all the children of Israel when they came up out of Egypt. So the Kenites departed. The Most High discriminates righteously: the people who showed Israel kindness were spared out of the judgment.

Saul smote the Amalekites from Havilah until thou comest to Shur, and utterly destroyed the people with the edge of the sword; but he took Agag the king of the Amalekites alive. He halfway fulfilled the order, reasoning like the king might be valuable as a hostage, as if the Lord forgot that detail. But Saul and the people spared Agag, and the best of the sheep, and of the oxen, and of the fatlings, and the lambs, and all that was good, and would not utterly destroy them; but every thing that was vile and refuse, that they destroyed utterly. They killed what looked like it deserved killing, so they could say they did some killing, and kept the healthy, good looking animals, telling themselves surely the Lord could not have meant these.

Then came the word of the Lord unto Samuel: It repenteth me that I have set up Saul to be king, for he is turned back from following me, and hath not performed my commandments. Mark the language: Saul did most of what was said, yet the Lord counts it as turning back and not performing his commandments at all. For everybody who says, well, I did do this part, understand: whenever there is a but in your obedience, you did not perform the orders given unto you. That is what the Most High is showing us in this story. And it grieved Samuel, and he cried unto the Lord all night. Pride had to be in operation for Saul to transgress on that level, and pride is where the throne is lost.

Samuel rose early to meet Saul, and it was told him that Saul came to Carmel and set him up a place, a monument to himself, and is gone down to Gilgal. When your transgression becomes the lesson, be thankful when the correction comes quietly and nobody knows your name; do not take the spirit of bitterness, because you deserved a lot more. Saul greets Samuel first with a cover: Blessed be thou of the Lord: I have performed the commandment of the Lord. The first thing out of his mouth is a fabrication, knowing full well he transgressed. Samuel answers, What meaneth then this bleating of the sheep in mine ears, and the lowing of the oxen which I hear? If you performed the commandment, why do I hear animals? Saul deflects again, the same blame game as chapter 13: They have brought them from the Amalekites, for the people spared the best of the sheep and of the oxen, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God; and the rest we have utterly destroyed. Verse 9 already told us Saul and the people spared them; now suddenly it is only the people, and for a good reason, a sacrifice, as though the Lord ought to be pleased.

Samuel said, Stay, and I will tell thee what the Lord hath said to me this night. When thou wast little in thine own sight, wast thou not made the head of the tribes of Israel, and the Lord anointed thee king over Israel? Samuel brings Saul back to his remembrance: when you thought nothing of yourself, with no confidence to be a ruler, the Most High still chose you. And the Lord sent thee on a journey, and said, Go and utterly destroy the sinners the Amalekites, and fight against them until they be consumed; the errand was the vengeance written in [Deuteronomy 25](/bible/deuteronomy/25). Wherefore then didst thou not obey the voice of the Lord, but didst fly upon the spoil, and didst evil in the sight of the Lord? Keeping the orders partially is evil in the sight of the Lord.

Saul is in denial: Yea, I have obeyed the voice of the lord, and have gone the way which the Lord sent me, and have brought Agag the king of Amalek, and have utterly destroyed the Amalekites. Samuel breaks down the rebuke and Saul tells the prophet he is wrong. In justifying himself over the animals, Saul volunteers even more of his rebellion, boasting that he spared the king, as if that was the smart move everyone really wanted; then he lays the spoil on the people again: the people took of the spoil, sheep and oxen, the chief of the things which should have been utterly destroyed, to sacrifice unto the Lord thy God in Gilgal.

Samuel makes it plain: Hath the Lord as great delight in burnt offerings and sacrifices, as in obeying the voice of the Lord? Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to hearken than the fat of rams. Do you think the Lord prefers a sacrifice to atone for broken commandments over you simply keeping the commandments? That is a heavy verse.

For rebellion is as the sin of witchcraft, and stubbornness is as iniquity and idolatry. That is heavy. A brother who would never touch voodoo will sit through a whole counsel of do not do this, and call two weeks later saying he did it anyway; according to this verse, that rebellion is the same as witchcraft. Stubbornness is idolatry because the instruction does not come from the man; it is the commandment of the Lord that leadership carries. When you are stubborn against it, you are saying what I want to do comes before what God wants me to do, and you have put yourself in the midst of idolatry as surely as circling the stone at Mecca or bowing before a cross. Because thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, he hath also rejected thee from being king: you will lose whatever position the Most High put you in. This stubborn heart is what fares evil at the last; we will read Saul's end in the last chapter of 1 Samuel, and in chapter 16 the evil spirit enters into him and the Spirit of the Lord departs. The plant of wickedness took root here.

Now the confession finally comes, and it is still not sincere: I have sinned, for I have transgressed the commandment of the Lord and thy words; because I feared the people, and obeyed their voice. Even in admitting it he deflects: it is the fault of the wicked people you put me over. Then he asks, Pardon my sin, and turn again with me, that I may worship the Lord; take me back to the regular Saul and Samuel connection, as though a fearful excuse settles it.

Samuel refuses: I will not return with thee; for thou hast rejected the word of the Lord, and the Lord hath rejected thee from being king over Israel. Think it through: Samuel gave Saul the opening at the bleating of the sheep, and Saul would not humble down; he asked why Saul disobeyed the voice of the Lord, and Saul justified himself again. Two admonitions were given and refused before this rejection.

As Samuel turned about to go away, Saul laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent. And Samuel said, The Lord hath rent the kingdom of Israel from thee this day, and hath given it to a neighbour of thine, that is better than thou. Just as Saul tore the hem of the garment, so the Lord tore the throne from him; and Samuel says this still before he has ever met David, the same word he gave in chapter 13. And also the Strength of Israel will not lie nor repent: for he is not a man, that he should repent. The Strength of Israel is the Most High. Understand the spirit of the title: whenever you go off on your own mind, pride has you departing from your strength, and once you have left your strength you are open to Satan; if a brother tells you that you are battling with pride, take heed and examine yourself.

Then he said, I have sinned: yet honour me now, I pray thee, before the elders of my people, and before Israel. This spirit is very real: okay, you are right, but do not let the people see the demotion; make sure they still know I am the king. That is the spirit of vanity, caught up in a rank and a title while forgetting that the title came for pleasing the Lord; once you discontinue pleasing the Lord, the title is going to leave as well. So Samuel turned again after Saul, and Saul worshipped the Lord.

Then said Samuel, Bring ye hither to me Agag the king of the Amalekites. And Agag came unto him delicately, and said, Surely the bitterness of death is past; with Saul under rebuke, Agag figured nobody was mad at the Amalekites anymore and he was safe. And Samuel said, As thy sword hath made women childless, so shall thy mother be childless among women. And Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord in Gilgal. The old prophet did not play; he finished the commandment himself, measure for measure for what Amalek's sword had done.

Then Samuel went to Ramah, and Saul went up to his house in Gibeah, and Samuel came no more to see Saul until the day of his death: nevertheless Samuel mourned for Saul, and the Lord repented that he had made Saul king over Israel. The mourning is what makes it sad: Samuel raised Saul up from nothing, saw his potential, and saw the Spirit come upon him in chapter 11 when he stood up as a savior for the people; he had hope in him, and it came to this. Samuel was grieved, and the Lord repented of the appointment. --- Topics: [Esau and Edom](/encyclopedia/esau-and-edom) · [Idolatry](/encyclopedia/idolatry) · [Sacrifice and Atonement](/encyclopedia/sacrifice-and-atonement) · [The Covenant](/encyclopedia/the-covenant) · [The Feasts of the Most High](/encyclopedia/the-feasts-of-the-most-high) · [The Priesthood](/encyclopedia/the-priesthood)

While David and his men were away with Achish, the Amalekites invaded the south and Ziklag, smote Ziklag and burned it with fire, and carried the women captive; they slew not any, great or small, but carried them away. David and his men came to the city on the third day, found it burned, and their wives and sons and daughters taken captive; they lifted up their voice and wept until they had no more power to weep. David's two wives were taken, Ahinoam the Jezreelitess and Abigail the wife of Nabal the Carmelite. David was greatly distressed, for the people spake of stoning him, because the soul of all the people was grieved, every man for his sons and his daughters; but David encouraged himself in the Lord his God. Notice how this connects to yesterday's reading in chapter 27. Achish had given David Ziklag, and David and his men had gone up and invaded the Amalekites and the other old inhabitants of the land, leaving neither man nor woman alive. Now the Amalekites came back and smote Ziklag the same way, taking David's wives and the families of his men while they were gone up with Achish.

David said to Abiathar the priest, Ahimelech's son, Bring hither the ephod, and David inquired at the Lord: shall I pursue after this troop? shall I overtake them? The answer came, Pursue: for thou shalt surely overtake them, and without fail recover all. David sought the Lord first and asked whether this thing was so before he moved; the Lord said go down, and you will recover.

David went, he and the six hundred men that were with him, and came to the brook Besor, where those that were left behind stayed. David pursued with four hundred men, for two hundred abode behind, which were so faint that they could not go over the brook Besor.

They found an Egyptian in the field and brought him to David; they gave him bread, water, a piece of a cake of figs, and two clusters of raisins, and when he had eaten his spirit came again to him, for he had eaten no bread nor drunk any water three days and three nights. A sidebar worth saying: this man was faint because he had gone without food three days and three nights. Some of our people are like that after fasting one day on the last Friday of the month; we have got to check our spirits. He was a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite, left behind because he fell sick three days before; his company had invaded the south of the Cherethites, the coast of Judah, and the south of Caleb, and burned Ziklag with fire. David asked, Canst thou bring me down to this company? He answered, Swear unto me by God that thou wilt neither kill me nor deliver me into the hands of my master, and I will bring thee down to this company.

When he had brought him down, behold, the Amalekites were spread abroad upon all the earth, eating and drinking and dancing because of all the great spoil they had taken out of the land of the Philistines and out of the land of Judah. David smote them from the twilight even unto the evening of the next day, and there escaped not a man of them, save four hundred young men which rode upon camels and fled. David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away, and rescued his two wives; there was nothing lacking to them, neither small nor great, neither sons nor daughters, neither spoil nor any thing that they had taken. David took all the flocks and the herds, and they said, This is David's spoil.

When David came back to the two hundred men at the brook Besor, all the wicked men and men of Belial among those that went with David said, Because they went not with us, we will not give them ought of the spoil that we have recovered, save every man his wife and his children. Notice these were David's own men, yet the scripture calls them wicked men and men of Belial; David called that thinking of the devil, saying they had the devil on them for even thinking like that. That is the same spirit a lot of our people have today: I went down there, my hands got me this, you have got to get your own. David said, Ye shall not do so, my brethren, with that which the Lord hath given us, who hath preserved us and delivered the company that came against us into our hand. The ruling: as his part is that goeth down to the battle, so shall his part be that tarrieth by the stuff; they shall part alike. Those that went down into the battle split the spoil with those that stayed behind, and from that day forward David made it a statute and an ordinance for Israel unto this day.

When David came to Ziklag he sent of the spoil unto the elders of Judah, even to his friends, saying, Behold a present for you of the spoil of the enemies of the Lord. The spoil went to them in Bethel, in south Ramoth, in Jattir, in Aroer, in Siphmoth, in Eshtemoa, in Rachal, in the cities of the Jerahmeelites, in the cities of the Kenites, in Hormah, in Chorashan, in Athach, in Hebron, and to all the places where David himself and his men were wont to haunt. The chapter in sum: the Amalekites spoiled the city and took the families while the men were gone up with Achish; David sought the Lord first, was told to pursue and recover, and went down and recovered all; and when his men that fought did not want to share with the men that were too faint, David made everybody part alike.

The sons of Judah and the families that came from them are set down, including the line of Hur, the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem. The names here carry meaning, and the record keeps the families in order down to the sons of Koz.

Jabez was more honorable than his brethren, and his mother called his name Jabez because she bare him with sorrow, the meaning of the name matching the scripture itself. Jabez called on the God of Israel and asked that He would bless him indeed, enlarge his coast, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil, and the Most High granted him what he requested.

The families of Judah are traced further through Chelub, Kenaz, Othniel, and the sons of Ezra and their households. The record names the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh and other households, and the names in this stretch carry meaning, as Jekuthiel was noted to point to the hope of the congregation of God.

The sons of Shelah the son of Judah are named, with the families that wrought fine linen and the potters that dwelt with the king for his work. These are called the ancient things, the old record of the trades and dwellings of these families.

The sons of Simeon are set down, and the record notes that Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brethren had not many children. Simeon did not multiply like the children of Judah, showing that the blessing of increase rested on Judah. Their dwellings at Beersheba and the surrounding cities are named, the same inheritance given to Simeon in Joshua. -

The princes of Simeon are named by their families, whose houses increased greatly, and they went to seek pasture for their flocks. They found fat and quiet pasture in a land where the sons of Ham had dwelt of old, and in the days of Hezekiah they smote those habitations and dwelt in their place. Five hundred of the sons of Simeon went to mount Seir, smote the remnant of the Amalekites that had escaped, and dwelt there, showing the Most High's blessing on them in war.

When Balaam saw that it pleased the Lord to bless Israel, he went not to seek enchantments, and the spirit of God came upon him. Do not be confused at the spirit of God coming on a man of another nation: all the spirits belong to the Most High, and He can do what He wants with any of them. That does not make the other nations prophets. Prophets are raised up of the sons of Israel; the Lord used Balaam for one specific purpose, to show the nations there is nothing they can do against Israel when the Lord is on our side, and to have Moses write it down in a book.

Balaam heard the words of God and saw the vision of the Almighty, falling into a trance, but having his eyes open. Picture a man staring off as if daydreaming: he is seeing visions with his eyes open while the Lord gives him what to say to the nations that are trying to do evil to Israel.

He shall pour the water out of his buckets, and his seed shall be in many waters. The water is the word: Christ sanctifies and cleanses the church with the washing of water by the word, and a young man cleanses his way by taking heed thereto according to the word. That is how you cleanse your spirit. His seed shall be in many waters means Israel scattered all over the earth, and his kingdom shall be exalted higher than Agag.

God brought him forth out of Egypt with as it were the strength of an unicorn; he shall eat up the nations his enemies, break their bones, and pierce them through with his arrows. That is the destruction coming on Israel's enemies when we rise back up. He couched, he lay down as a great lion, and who shall stir him up? Blessed is he that blesseth thee, and cursed is he that curseth thee. Balaam is speaking the very prophecies and promises that belong to Israel throughout the scriptures.

Balak's anger was kindled and he smote his hands together: I thought to promote thee unto great honour, but lo, the Lord hath kept thee back from honour. That was Satan speaking through Balak, trying to entice Balaam with honor to curse Israel. Satan promotes with honor, riches, prestige, and lust; that is the deceitfulness of riches and the lust of other things that choke the word. When the word is sown, Satan comes immediately to take it away, using whatever device fits where you are. He tried the same device on Christ, offering all the power and the glory of the kingdoms in exchange for worship, and Christ answered, Get thee behind me, Satan. Satan is an old spirit using the same tricks from the beginning of time. We are not to be ignorant of his devices, lest he get an advantage of us. Many are falling to those devices at home in this quarantine, letting the old man rise back up; resist the devil and he will flee, but give in and he will use you until he destroys you.

Balaam answered: if Balak would give me his house full of silver and gold, I cannot go beyond the commandment of the Lord, to do either good or bad of mine own mind; but what the Lord saith, that will I speak.

Behold, I go unto my people: Balaam's people were the Midianites, for Israel later slew Balaam with the sword beside the five kings of Midian. I will advertise thee what this people shall do to thy people in the latter days. The latter days are the last days, and the last days began when Christ came on the earth, was crucified, and resurrected: God, who spake in time past unto the fathers by the prophets, hath in these last days spoken unto us by His Son. A thousand years is as a day to the Lord, and a day as a thousand years; as Hosea says, after two days He will revive us, and in the third day He will raise us up. The full teaching of that timing belongs to another class.

I shall see him, but not now: I shall behold him, but not nigh. Balaam is saying the Most High will raise him up again in the last days, but as a servant, far off from the King; he will behold him, but he will not be near him. Compare that with Job, and the contrast shows Job was an Israelite and not of another nation: Job knew that his redeemer liveth, that in his flesh he shall see God, whom he shall see for himself and his eyes shall behold, and not another. Balaam has no such nearness, because the redeemer is not his. There shall come a Star out of Jacob: the Star is Christ, the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star. And a Sceptre shall rise out of Israel: the sceptre belongs to kings, so the prophecy is that the King shall rise out of Israel.

And Edom shall be a possession. Edom is nowhere named in the matter of Balak and Balaam in these chapters, but the Lord made sure Edom was written into the prophecy: Seir also shall be a possession for his enemies, and Israel shall do valiantly. The law of bondmen shows what a possession is: the heathen round about are bought for an inheritance, bondmen for ever, though over our own brethren we do not rule with rigour. For Esau that servitude is not for ever, because Esau is the only nation on the earth with an expiration date. The house of Jacob, the twelve tribes of Israel, the blacks, Hispanics, and Native Indians, shall be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau for stubble; there shall not be any remaining of the house of Esau, for the Lord hath spoken it. The rest of the nations go into servitude for ever, but the Lord can only bear with Esau so much longer. Out of Jacob shall come he that shall have dominion: that is the one who cometh from Edom with dyed garments from Bozrah, glorious in his apparel, traveling in the greatness of his strength, which is the whole host of heaven, thousands upon thousands of angels. The day of vengeance is in his heart, for though Israel serves out her punishment in captivity, Esau went overboard and kept laying on punishment when our iniquity had an end.

Amalek was the first of the nations. That means Amalek was the first of the nations to come out and fight against Israel, when he met us at Rephidim as we came out of Egypt. The Lord swore to utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven, and that the Lord would have war with Amalek from generation to generation. This teaching identifies Amalek, the seed of Esau through Eliphaz, with the people who call themselves Jewish in the land of Israel today: the war that has never left that land since they entered it is the war the Lord swore, and the prophecy that none shall remain of the house of Esau belongs to no other nation. His latter end shall be that he perish for ever; precept upon precept, the scriptures show who Amalek is and what his end is.
The Kenite's dwelling place was strong, his nest put in a rock; nevertheless the Kenite shall be wasted and go into captivity, until Asshur, which is the Assyrians, shall carry him away captive.

Alas, who shall live when God doeth this! Ships shall come from the coast of Chittim, and Chittim is Italy; they shall afflict Asshur and afflict Eber, and he also shall perish for ever. Eber here is not speaking of Israel, for other peoples besides us came out of Eber, who is of Shem; the history of prophecy opens this up as the prophets are read. And Balaam rose up and returned to his place, and Balak also went his way; they parted.

text.text: Then came Amalek, and fought with Israel in Rephidim.
And Moses said unto Joshua, Choose us out men, and go out, fight with Amalek: to morrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in mine hand.
So Joshua did as Moses had said to him, and fought with Amalek: and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill.
And it came to pass, when Moses held up his hand, that Israel prevailed: and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed.

But Moses’ hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat thereon; and Aaron and Hur stayed up his hands, the one on the one side, and the other on the other side; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
And Joshua discomfited Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword.
And the Lord said unto Moses, Write this for a memorial in a book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua: for I will utterly put out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven.
And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it JEHOVAH–nissi:
For he said, Because the Lord hath sworn that the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation.
Remember what Amalek did unto thee by the way, when ye were come forth out of Egypt;
How he met thee by the way, and smote the hindmost of thee, even all that were feeble behind thee, when thou wast faint and weary; and he feared not God.

Therefore it shall be, when the Lord thy God hath given thee rest from all thine enemies round about, in the land which the Lord thy God giveth thee for an inheritance to possess it, that thou shalt blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven; thou shalt not forget it.
Thus saith the Lord of hosts, I remember that which Amalek did to Israel, how he laid wait for him in the way, when he came up from Egypt.
Now go and smite Amalek, and utterly destroy all that they have, and spare them not; but slay both man and woman, infant and suckling, ox and sheep, camel and ass.
And David smote them from the twilight even unto the evening of the next day: and there escaped not a man of them, save four hundred young men, which rode upon camels, and fled.
And David recovered all that the Amalekites had carried away: and David rescued his two wives.
And some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, and Neariah, and Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
And they smote the rest of the Amalekites that were escaped, and dwelt there unto this day.
And when he looked on Amalek, he took up his parable, and said, Amalek was the first of the nations; but his latter end shall be that he perish for ever.
